questions.stem: This question is about the states of matter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The diagram shows the three states of matter for a substance. solid liquid gas Each circle represents a molecule of the substance.

parts.label: a-i
parts.text: Complete the diagram by drawing six circles to represent molecules in the gas state.

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: Which statement is correct about the movement or arrangement of the molecules of this substance? A They move randomly in the solid state. B They move randomly in the liquid state. C They are arranged in fixed positions in the liquid state. D They are arranged in fixed positions in the gas state.

parts.label: a-iii
parts.text: Which term is used for a solid changing to a liquid? A boiling B condensing freezing D melting

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some cold water is poured into a conical flask and a bung inserted. The diagram shows the flask after a few minutes.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: What is occurring in the flask? A boiling and condensing B condensing and evaporating C evaporating and freezing D freezing and melting

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Which formula represents a substance that is not present in the flask? A $ \mathrm{H_{2}O(g)} $ B $ \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} $ C $ \mathrm{N_{2}(g)} $ D $ \mathrm{N_{2}(l)} $

questions.stem: A teacher demonstrates, in a fume cupboard, two experiments to show the movement of particles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the first experiment she places some liquid bromine at the bottom of a gas jar. She then places another gas jar containing air on top of it, as shown in the diagram. The diagram shows the apparatus at the start, after a few minutes and at the end of the experiment. Place crosses ( $ \times $ ) in two boxes to show which statements are correct about this experiment. A All the air particles in the upper gas jar stay there. B Bromine and air react to form bromine oxide. C Bromine has a darker colour than air. D Bromine vapour diffuses upwards. E Liquid bromine sublimes during the experiment. F The concentration of bromine in the lower gas jar does not change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the second experiment, she soaks two pieces of cotton wool in different liquids and places them at opposite ends of a glass tube. She immediately seals the tube with bungs. The diagram shows the apparatus at the start of the experiment. During the experiment a white ring appears in the tube.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: State whether the white ring appears at A, B or C.

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Explain your choice.

questions.stem: Magnesium is an element in Group 2 of the Periodic Table. When magnesium burns in air it forms magnesium oxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two observations made when magnesium burns in air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnesium oxide is A an acidic oxide formed from a metal B an acidic oxide formed from a non-metal C a basic oxide formed from a metal D a basic oxide formed from a non-metal

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some magnesium oxide is tested with damp litmus paper.

parts.label: c-i
parts.text: State the final colour of the litmus paper.

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: Identify the ion responsible for this colour.

questions.stem: A student adds dilute sulfuric acid to a beaker containing calcium chloride solution. He obtains a mixture containing a precipitate of calcium sulfate in a solution of hydrochloric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the equation for this reaction by inserting state symbols. $\mathrm {C a C l} _ {2} (\dots \dots \dots \dots \dots) + \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {S O} _ {4} (\dots \dots \dots \dots) \rightarrow \mathrm {C a S O} _ {4} (\dots \dots \dots \dots) + 2 \mathrm {H C l} (\dots \dots \dots \dots)$

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student uses this apparatus to separate the mixture into a residue and a filtrate. Draw a diagram to show how he should assemble the apparatus for the filtration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student carries out a flame test on the filtrate he obtains and observes a brick-red colour.

parts.label: c-i
parts.text: Identify the ion responsible for this colour.

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: Suggest why this ion is present in the filtrate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The student tests the filtrate for chloride ions by adding silver nitrate solution.

parts.label: d-i
parts.text: State what he would observe in this test.

parts.label: d-ii
parts.text: State the name of the substance responsible for this observation.

parts.label: d-iii
parts.text: He reads in a textbook that dilute nitric acid should be added before the silver nitrate solution in the test. Suggest why the student does not need to add dilute nitric acid in the test.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The calcium sulfate residue he obtains is impure because it contains some hydrochloric acid. Describe how he can obtain a pure dry sample of calcium sulfate from this residue.

questions.stem: The table shows the displayed formulae of six organic compounds, P, Q, R, S, T and U.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the molecular formula of compound S?

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: What is the empirical formula of compound T?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the letters of two compounds that belong to the homologous series of alkenes.

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: The general formula of this homologous series is A $ C_{n}H_{2 n-2} $ B $ C_{n}H_{2 n+2} $ C $ C_{n}+H_{2 n} $ D $ C_{n}H_{2 n} $

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which of these conversions is an example of an addition reaction? A compound P $ \rightarrow $ compound Q B compound Q $ \rightarrow $ compound T C compound R $ \rightarrow $ compound Q D compound R -> compound U

parts.label: d
parts.text: Complete the table to show the displayed formula and name of the isomer of compound T.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The equation represents a reaction between compound P and bromine.

parts.label: e-i
parts.text: Complete the equation to show the displayed formula of the organic product.

parts.label: e-ii
parts.text: State the name of this organic product.

parts.label: e-iii
parts.text: State the condition used in this reaction.

parts.label: e-iv
parts.text: What term is used for this type of reaction? A addition B hydration neutralisation substitution

parts.label: f
parts.text: Old refrigerators may contain substances that harm the ozone layer in the atmosphere. Many new refrigerators use 152a, an organic compound that does not harm the ozone layer. 152a has the composition by mass C=36.4% , H=6.0% and F=57.6%.

parts.label: f-i
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of 152a. empirical formula

parts.label: f-ii
parts.text: The relative formula mass of 152a is 66 What is its molecular formula?

questions.stem: The diagram shows a typical fractionating column used to separate crude oil into fractions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The diagram shows the names of some of the fractions. State the name of fraction A and the name of fraction F. fraction A fraction F

parts.label: b
parts.text: Most compounds in crude oil are hydrocarbons. State the meaning of the term hydrocarbons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the boiling point, colour and viscosity of the fuel oil fraction differ from those of the gasoline fraction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Some fuel oil undergoes catalytic cracking. This involves the conversion of long-chain alkanes into alkenes and short-chain alkanes.

parts.label: d-i
parts.text: A temperature of about $ 6 5 0^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ is used in this process. Identify a catalyst that is used.

parts.label: d-ii
parts.text: The alkane tridecane can be cracked to produce octane and two different alkenes. Complete the equation to show the formulae of the two alkenes. $\mathrm {C} _ {1 3} \mathrm {H} _ {2 8} \rightarrow \mathrm {C} _ {8} \mathrm {H} _ {1 8} +$

parts.label: e
parts.text: When hydrocarbons undergo incomplete combustion, a poisonous gas can form.

parts.label: e-i
parts.text: State the condition that causes incomplete combustion.

parts.label: e-ii
parts.text: Identify the poisonous gas.

parts.label: e-iii
parts.text: Explain why this gas is poisonous.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Another problem with using hydrocarbon fuels is the formation of substances that cause an environmental problem. This sequence of equations shows how one of these substances forms. $S + O _ {2} \rightarrow S O _ {2}$ $2 \mathrm {S O} _ {2} + \mathrm {O} _ {2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm {S O} _ {3}$ $\mathrm {S O} _ {3} + \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} \rightarrow \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {S O} _ {4}$

parts.label: f-i
parts.text: State the name of the product of each of these reactions. $\mathrm {S O} _ {2}$ $\mathrm {S O} _ {3}$ $\mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {S O} _ {4}$

parts.label: f-ii
parts.text: Describe one environmental problem caused by the $ \mathrm{H_{2} S O_{4}} $ formed.

questions.stem: This question is about polymers. The formation of poly(ethene) can be represented as

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the name of this type of reaction? A addition B decomposition substitution C reduction

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which of these is a correct description of a monomer? C an atom in a polymer A a molecule used to make a polymer

parts.label: c
parts.text: This compound is used to make a polymer. B a molecule with only single bonds D a repeat unit in a polymer

parts.label: c-i
parts.text: State the name of this compound.

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: Draw the structure of the repeat unit of the polymer formed from this compound.

parts.label: d
parts.text: This is part of the structure of another polymer. Draw the displayed formula of the monomer used to make this polymer.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Many polymers do not biodegrade when they are thrown away.

parts.label: e-i
parts.text: State the meaning of the term biodegrade.

parts.label: e-ii
parts.text: What property of these polymers prevents them from biodegrading?

questions.stem: A student carries out a titration to find the concentration of some dilute sulfuric acid. She is given a supply of the dilute sulfuric acid sodium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.150 mol/dm $ ^{3} $ apparatus suitable for carrying out a titration phenolphthalein indicator She uses this method to do the titration. step 1 add 25.0 $ cm^{3} $ of the sodium hydroxide solution to a conical flask step 2 add 3 drops of phenolphthalein indicator to the conical flask step 3 fill a burette with the sulfuric acid step 4 add the sulfuric acid to the conical flask until the phenolphthalein indicator just changes colour

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the piece of apparatus that the student should use to add the sodium hydroxide solution in step 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is the colour change of the phenolphthalein indicator in step 4? A colourless to pink B pink to colourless C red to yellow D yellow to red

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why is it better to use phenolphthalein indicator rather than universal indicator in this titration?

parts.label: d
parts.text: The diagram shows the burette readings in one titration. Use the readings to complete the table, entering all values to the nearest 0.05 $ cm^{3}. $

parts.label: e
parts.text: The student repeats the experiment using the same sodium hydroxide solution but another solution of sulfuric acid of a different concentration. The table shows her results. The average (mean) volume of acid should be calculated using only concordant results. Concordant results are those volumes that differ from each other by 0.20 $ cm^{3} $ or less.

parts.label: e-i
parts.text: Identify the concordant results by placing ticks ( $ \surd $ ) in the table where appropriate.

parts.label: e-ii
parts.text: Use your ticked results to calculate the average volume of acid added.

parts.label: f
parts.text: The student uses a similar method to find the concentration of a solution of phosphoric acid $ \left( \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{P O}_{4} \right) $ The equation for the reaction is $3 \mathrm {N a O H} + \mathrm {H} _ {3} \mathrm {P O} _ {4} \rightarrow \mathrm {N a} _ {3} \mathrm {P O} _ {4} + 3 \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O}$ The table shows her results.

parts.label: f-i
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in moles, of NaOH in $ 2 5. 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of the sodium hydroxide solution. $\mathrm {a m o u n t o f N a O H} =$

parts.label: f-ii
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in moles, of $ \mathrm{H_{3} P O_{4}} $ in the phosphoric acid solution. $\mathrm {a m o u n t o f H} _ {3} \mathrm {P O} _ {4} =$

parts.label: f-iii
parts.text: Calculate the concentration, in mol/dm $ ^{3} $ , of the phosphoric acid. $\mathrm {m o l / d m ^ {3}}$

questions.stem: This question is about bonding, structures and properties.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The box gives four types of structure. The table shows some properties of four substances, A, B, C and D. Complete the table by giving the correct type of structure for each substance. You may use each structure once, more than once or not at all.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnesium chloride $ \left(\mathrm{M g C l}_{2}\right) $ is an ionic compound. The diagram shows the electronic configurations of atoms of magnesium and chlorine.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: Describe how magnesium atoms and chlorine atoms form magnesium ions and chloride ions.

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Draw a diagram to represent the electronic configurations of each of the ions in magnesium chloride. Show the charge on each ion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A molecule of carbon dioxide contains double covalent bonds. Complete the diagram, using dots and crosses, to show the arrangement of the outer electrons in a molecule of carbon dioxide.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Indium is a metal in Group 3 of the Periodic Table.

parts.label: d-i
parts.text: Describe the structure and bonding in indium.

parts.label: d-ii
parts.text: Explain why indium is malleable.

questions.stem: A student investigates the rate of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide solution. The diagram shows the apparatus he uses in his experiments. The equation for the decomposition is $2 \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} _ {2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} + \mathrm {O} _ {2}$

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student keeps the amount, in moles, of $ \mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}} $ in the solution constant at the start of each experiment. State two properties of the solution that he should keep the same to ensure that the amount of $ \mathrm{H_{2} O_{2}} $ is the same in each experiment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student carries out the experiment five times. He uses a different solid in each experiment to see how effective each solid is as a catalyst in the decomposition. He removes the bung, adds a small amount of one of the solids and quickly replaces the bung. He records the time taken to collect 100 $ cm^{3} $ of oxygen in the syringe.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: Which solid does not seem to act as a catalyst?

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Which solid is the most effective catalyst?

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the first experiment the student added 1 g of solid A. Describe what he could do with the contents of the conical flask at the end of the experiment to show that A was a catalyst, and not a reactant.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The student repeats the experiment using the same apparatus, but this time he records the volume of oxygen collected at intervals of 20 seconds. The table shows his results for two new solids F and G.

parts.label: d-i
parts.text: The grid shows the results plotted for solid F. On the grid, plot the results for solid G. Draw a curve of best fit. Volume of oxygen in $ \mathrm{c m}^{3} $

parts.label: d-ii
parts.text: Use your graph to estimate the volume of oxygen collected after 70 seconds for solid G. Show on your graph how you obtained your answer.

parts.label: d-iii
parts.text: How do the curves on the graph show that the reaction is faster with solid F than with solid G?

questions.stem: A manufacturer investigates some reactions that produce hydrogen. The table shows three possible reversible reactions that he could use. The enthalpy changes are also shown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For reaction 1, predict whether the pressure should be low or high to give the greatest yield of products.

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: Give a reason for your choice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For reaction 1, predict whether the temperature should be low or high to give the greatest yield of products.

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Give a reason for your choice.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For reaction 2, suggest why changing the temperature will have less effect on the yield of products than in reactions 1 and 3.

parts.label: d
parts.text: For reaction 3, predict the effect on the rate of the forward reaction of increasing the pressure, without changing the temperature.

parts.label: d-ii
parts.text: Explain your prediction in terms of the particle collision theory.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The manufacturer makes a batch of ethanoic acid from methanol and carbon monoxide using this reaction. $\mathrm {C H} _ {3} \mathrm {O H} + \mathrm {C O} \rightarrow \mathrm {C H} _ {3} \mathrm {C O O H}$ He starts with 64kg of methanol.
